metadata.description: Learn 20 possible stomach cancer warning signs, the major risk factors, how stomach cancer is investigated and what can affect treatment and outlook.
metadata.title: 20 Stomach Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore

landing.title: 20 Stomach Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
landing.intro: Some are surprisingly easy to dismiss as indigestion — including several signs people often miss.

icon.alt: Woman holding her painful upper abdomen

disclaimer: General educational information only. These signs are common and usually have causes other than stomach cancer. They cannot diagnose or rule out cancer. New, persistent, worsening or unusual symptoms should be assessed by a qualified healthcare professional. Seek urgent medical help for vomiting blood, black or bloody stool, severe or rapidly worsening pain, repeated vomiting, fainting, or signs of a blockage or significant bleeding.

sections.title: 20 Stomach Cancer Warning Signs
sections.intro: Stomach cancer often causes no symptoms early on. When changes do appear, they can look like common digestive problems, so persistence and a change from what is normal for you matter.

points.title: Indigestion that does not settle
paragraphs: Repeated discomfort, burning or heaviness after eating may feel like ordinary indigestion. It is usually caused by something less serious, but a new pattern that persists despite usual treatment deserves assessment.

points.title: Heartburn or acid reflux that changes
paragraphs: Acid rising into the chest or throat is very common. Speak with a healthcare professional when reflux is new, worsening, unusually frequent or no longer responds as it normally does.

points.title: Burping much more than usual
paragraphs: Frequent belching can form part of persistent indigestion. On its own it rarely indicates cancer, but it is worth mentioning when it arrives with pain, early fullness, appetite loss or other continuing changes.

points.title: Bloating after eating
paragraphs: A swollen or uncomfortably full feeling after meals can have many dietary and digestive explanations. A persistent pattern that is new for you should not simply be assumed to be normal.

points.title: Feeling full after only a small amount
paragraphs: You may find that a few mouthfuls make you feel unable to continue eating. This is called early satiety and needs assessment when it continues or contributes to appetite or weight changes.

points.title: Losing your appetite
paragraphs: Food may seem less appealing, or you may repeatedly leave meals unfinished. Stress, infection and many other conditions can affect appetite, but a lasting unexplained change warrants a conversation.

points.title: Nausea that keeps returning
paragraphs: Feeling sick can follow infection, medicines, reflux and many other problems. Recurrent or persistent nausea matters more when it appears with pain, fullness, vomiting or weight loss.

points.title: Repeated vomiting
paragraphs: Vomiting that continues can lead to dehydration and may signal a blockage or another condition needing prompt care. Do not wait for it to become severe before seeking medical advice.

points.title: Difficulty swallowing
paragraphs: Food or drink may feel slow to pass, painful to swallow or stuck on the way down. Problems swallowing should be medically assessed rather than managed by simply changing what you eat.

points.title: Pain in the upper abdomen
paragraphs: An ache, pressure or pain near the top of the abdomen can come from the stomach or several nearby organs. New pain that persists, worsens or appears with other symptoms needs checking.

next.title: There Are 10 More You Should Know
next.copy: The next signs include bleeding, anaemia and changes that may appear when stomach cancer is more advanced.

sections.title: More Stomach Cancer Warning Signs Worth Knowing
sections.intro: These changes still do not prove that cancer is present. Some are more concerning or may occur later, which makes timely medical assessment particularly important.

points.title: A persistent discomfort above the belly button
paragraphs: Some people describe a vague soreness, pressure or unsettled sensation rather than sharp pain. A continuing change in the upper middle abdomen deserves assessment even when it is difficult to describe.

points.title: Losing weight without trying
paragraphs: Unintentional weight loss has many possible causes. It should be discussed promptly when it is noticeable, continuing or accompanied by appetite loss, early fullness or digestive symptoms.

points.title: Unusual tiredness or low energy
paragraphs: Persistent fatigue can occur if slow bleeding leads to anaemia, although sleep problems and many common illnesses can do the same. Blood tests can help identify the cause.

points.title: Weakness, paleness or breathlessness
paragraphs: Too few red blood cells can leave someone weak, pale, dizzy or short of breath. These changes require assessment because anaemia has many possible causes, including bleeding in the digestive tract.

points.title: Vomiting blood
paragraphs: Blood in vomit may look bright red or resemble dark coffee grounds. This can have causes other than cancer, but it is a warning sign that needs urgent medical attention.

points.title: Blood in the stool or black stool
paragraphs: Bleeding higher in the digestive tract can make stool look very dark, black or tar-like. Seek urgent medical advice rather than assuming a colour change is harmless.

points.title: A lump at the top of the abdomen
paragraphs: A new lump, firm area or swelling in the upper abdomen needs examination. Do not wait for it to become painful or increase in size before arranging care.

points.title: A swollen or tight abdomen
paragraphs: Fluid can sometimes build up in the abdomen when cancer is advanced, creating swelling, tight clothing or discomfort. Liver, heart and other conditions can also cause this and need prompt assessment.

points.title: Yellowing of the skin or eyes
paragraphs: Jaundice can occur if advanced cancer affects the liver, but it has many other possible causes. Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or pale stool should be assessed urgently.

points.title: A familiar digestive problem that becomes different
paragraphs: People with reflux or another long-term digestive condition may become used to symptoms. A pattern that changes, worsens, persists or no longer responds to usual treatment is worth discussing.

next.title: But Who Is Most At Risk?
next.copy: Symptoms are only part of the picture. Infection, age, family history and long-term changes in the stomach lining can all affect risk.

sections.title: Stomach Cancer Risk: 10 Things Worth Knowing
sections.intro: A risk factor is not a diagnosis. Many people with risk factors never develop stomach cancer, while others who are diagnosed have no obvious risk factor.

points.title: Getting older
paragraphs: Stomach cancer becomes more common with age, although it can occur in younger adults. Age is considered alongside symptoms, health and other risk factors.

points.title: Long-term Helicobacter pylori infection
paragraphs: Chronic infection with H. pylori can damage the stomach lining and raise the risk of some stomach cancers. Most infected people do not develop cancer, and treatment can reduce risk.

points.title: A close family history
paragraphs: Risk can be higher when a parent, sibling or child has had stomach cancer. The number of relatives, their ages at diagnosis and the exact cancer type all help put that history into context.

points.title: Inherited cancer syndromes
paragraphs: Rare inherited changes, including those linked with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer or Lynch syndrome, can increase risk. A strong family pattern may prompt genetic counselling rather than assumptions based on one relative.

points.title: Chronic atrophic gastritis or intestinal metaplasia
paragraphs: Long-standing inflammation can thin or change the stomach lining over time. These findings require individual advice about treatment and whether surveillance is appropriate.

points.title: Pernicious anaemia
paragraphs: This autoimmune condition affects vitamin B12 absorption and is associated with changes in the stomach lining. It does not mean cancer is present, but it belongs in a clinician's assessment.

points.title: Previous stomach surgery or certain stomach polyps
paragraphs: Some previous operations and particular types of polyps can affect long-term risk. The reason for surgery, the tissue findings and the time since treatment all matter.

points.title: Smoking
paragraphs: Tobacco use is linked with a higher risk of stomach cancer as well as many other cancers. Stopping reduces health risks at any age.

points.title: Diet and alcohol patterns
paragraphs: Diets high in heavily salted, smoked or poorly preserved foods and heavier alcohol use are associated with increased risk. These are population-level patterns, not a diagnosis for an individual.

points.title: Body weight and reflux can matter by tumour location
paragraphs: Excess body weight and long-term reflux are more strongly associated with cancers near the upper stomach and the junction with the oesophagus. Risk varies by the exact site and wider health picture.

next.eyebrow: KNOW THE SIGNS. KNOW THE RISK.
next.title: So How Do Doctors Actually Check For It?
next.copy: Symptoms and risk factors cannot confirm stomach cancer. See how examination, endoscopy, biopsy and scans fit together.

sections.title: What Actually Happens During A Stomach Cancer Check?
sections.intro: The exact pathway depends on symptoms, history and local guidance. Not everyone needs every test, but the sequence below shows how a possible stomach cancer is commonly investigated.

points.title: Symptoms and medical or family history
paragraphs: A clinician asks what has changed, how long it has lasted, whether eating or swallowing is affected, and whether bleeding or weight loss is present. Medicines, H. pylori, previous stomach problems and family cancers may also matter.

points.title: Physical examination
paragraphs: The abdomen may be examined for tenderness, swelling or a lump. The clinician may also look for pallor, jaundice, dehydration or other signs that help determine urgency.

points.title: Blood and stool tests
paragraphs: Blood tests can look for anaemia and assess general health, while a stool test may detect hidden blood. These results can guide the next step but cannot diagnose stomach cancer on their own.

points.title: Upper endoscopy
paragraphs: A thin flexible camera is passed through the mouth to inspect the oesophagus, stomach and first part of the small intestine. Sedation is commonly used, and suspicious areas can be sampled during the procedure.

points.title: Biopsy and laboratory testing
paragraphs: A biopsy is needed to confirm whether cancer cells are present. If cancer is found, the tissue may be tested for features such as HER2, mismatch-repair status or other biomarkers that can affect treatment.

points.title: Scans and staging tests
paragraphs: CT, endoscopic ultrasound, PET or staging laparoscopy may be used depending on the situation. These tests assess how deeply a tumour has grown, nearby lymph nodes and whether it has spread elsewhere.

next.title: What Happens If Stomach Cancer Is Confirmed?
next.copy: The stage, exact location and laboratory features all shape what doctors may recommend next.

sections.title: Stomach Cancer Treatment And Outlook: What Really Matters
sections.intro: No single symptom or scan can predict what will happen. A specialist team combines the cancer's type, stage, position, laboratory features and the person's health before recommending treatment.

points.title: Where the cancer started
paragraphs: The exact part of the stomach and whether the tumour reaches the junction with the oesophagus can affect surgery, staging and the treatment plan.

points.title: How deeply it has grown
paragraphs: Stomach cancer begins in the inner lining and can grow into deeper layers or nearby structures. The depth of growth forms an important part of the stage.

points.title: Whether lymph nodes or distant organs are involved
paragraphs: Nearby lymph nodes, the liver, lungs and the lining of the abdomen are among the areas doctors may assess. Spread changes both the treatment aims and the options available.

points.title: Very early cancer may be removed through an endoscope
paragraphs: Selected cancers confined to the inner lining and judged unlikely to have spread may be suitable for endoscopic removal. This is not appropriate for every early tumour.

points.title: Surgery may remove part or all of the stomach
paragraphs: When a cancer can be removed, surgery may involve a subtotal or total gastrectomy with nearby lymph nodes. The operation depends on location and extent, and nutrition support is an important part of recovery.

points.title: Chemotherapy is often combined with surgery
paragraphs: Drug treatment may be given before surgery, after it or both. In advanced disease, chemotherapy can also help control cancer and relieve symptoms.

points.title: Radiotherapy can have a role
paragraphs: Radiotherapy may be combined with chemotherapy in some circumstances or used to control pain, bleeding or other symptoms when the disease cannot be removed.

points.title: Biomarkers can open targeted or immune-treatment options
paragraphs: Laboratory testing can identify features that make targeted medicines or immunotherapy relevant. The options continue to change and depend on the cancer's specific results.

points.title: General health, nutrition and personal priorities matter
paragraphs: Fitness, other medical conditions, ability to maintain nutrition and what matters most to the person influence which treatments are suitable. Supportive and palliative care can be used alongside cancer treatment at any stage.

points.title: Statistics describe groups, not individuals
paragraphs: Outlook depends strongly on stage and response to treatment, but population figures cannot predict one person's future. The specialist team can interpret the most current results in context.

conclusion.copy: Stomach symptoms are common and usually are not cancer, but a new, persistent or worsening pattern deserves assessment. Endoscopy and biopsy—not symptoms alone—are what establish a diagnosis, and doctors combine stage, tumour biology, health and treatment response when discussing outlook.
